metadata.note:
The Columbus & Hocking Valley Railroad, Columbus to Athens, Ohio - added 2026-08-27 at the user's request. Before this the dataset had nine lines within 12 km of Columbus but nothing at all at Lancaster, Logan or Nelsonville. Incorporated as the Mineral Rail Road in 1864 and renamed when Columbus money finished it in 1867, the C&HV opened in four steps between 16 July 1868 and 25 July 1870 and was built to move Hocking Valley salt and coal - but it carried passengers throughout, three trains a day each way at the peak. It consolidated in 1881 into the Columbus, Hocking Valley & Toledo, was reorganised in 1899 as the Hocking Valley Railway, and was merged into the Chesapeake & Ohio on 30 April 1930 as its Hocking Division. Passenger service on the C&O's lines east of Columbus ended on 31 December 1949. Passengers returned in 1972 with the volunteer Hocking Valley Scenic Railway, which since 1985 has run 12 mi of the original grade between Nelsonville and East Logan and is drawn here as mode 'tourist_rail'.

Only the C&HV's own Columbus-Athens line is drawn. The Columbus-Toledo line (Columbus & Toledo Railway, 1876-77) and the Logan-Gallipolis-Pomeroy line (Ohio & West Virginia Railway, 1880-81) came into the same company in 1881 but were built by different concerns and are not in this file. Neither are the Straitsville, Monday Creek and Snow Fork branches, which were coal lines - Rule 1.
metadata.geometry_source: OpenStreetMap, fetched 2026-08-27. Route relations 17423903 (Indiana & Ohio Logan Subdivision) and 17423809 (Hocking Valley Scenic Railway) pulled whole from the OSM API and chained by shared node ids, plus Overpass bbox dumps for the Columbus terminal approach and for the Nelsonville-Athens grade, the latter surviving as the Hockhocking Adena Bikeway and tagged old_railway_operator=C&O. Douglas-Peucker simplified at 25 m.
metadata.mileage_check: 75.43 mi Columbus-Athens against a documented ~75, with Canal Winchester at 15.4 mi, Lancaster 30.8, Logan 50.1, Nelsonville 62.0. Hocking Valley Scenic Railway 12.39 mi against a documented 12.
not_yet_sourced: The month of the 1881 consolidation into the Columbus, Hocking Valley & Toledo is a live conflict: Abandoned Online says July 1881, Wikipedia says August 1881. Neither has been checked against a primary source and the drawn year, 1881, is unaffected either way.
Every headway_min here is an estimate except the three-trains-a-day figure for the C&HV's Columbus-Athens service at its peak, and even that is not tied to a particular year.
The 31 December 1949 end of passenger service is sourced to the Hocking Valley Scenic Railway's own history and a Hawkins Rails page, not to a timetable or an ICC filing.

The Hocking Valley Scenic Railway's 1972-1985 routes - roughly seven miles of the Monday Creek branch to Carbon Hill until it was scrapped in 1983, then Nelsonville to Glen Ebon - are not drawn. Glen Ebon's location was not established.
The tourist railway's 720-minute headway is a placeholder. It runs weekends and seasonally, not daily, and this dataset has no field that expresses that.
The Columbus-Toledo and Logan-Gallipolis-Pomeroy lines of the same company, and the passenger service on them, are not covered.
The Columbus and Athens terminal approaches are not drawn: the line stops 1.35 km short of the Union Station site and 1.34 km short of the Athens depot site.
sources: https://abandonedonline.net/location/hocking-valley-railway/ (Mineral Rail Road incorporated 14 April 1864; Greene's 1867 purchase and the naming condition; 22 May 1867 construction contract; openings 16 July 1868 Canal Winchester, 13 January 1869 Lancaster, 17 August 1869 Nelsonville, 25 July 1870 Athens; Straitsville Branch 2 January 1871; Columbus & Toledo 1876-77; Ohio & West Virginia 1880-81; consolidation July 1881; C&O; Hocking Valley Scenic Railway route history)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hocking_Valley_Railway (C&T incorporated 1872; Gallipolis, McArthur & Columbus 1870; consolidation August 1881; receivership 1897 and February 1899 reorganisation as the Hocking Valley Railway; C&O control March 1910 and merger April 1930; 349 miles of road on 881 miles of track at the end of 1925; Toledo-Columbus now CSX's Columbus Subdivision)

https://www.hvsry.org/about/ (regular passenger service to Lancaster 1869; first freight from Nelsonville 17 August 1869 with the cannon; full service to Athens summer 1870; three daily passenger trains each way Columbus-Athens at the peak)
https://hawkinsrails.net/preservation/hvsr/hvsr.htm (Hocking Valley merged into the C&O 30 April 1930 as the Hocking Division; passenger service east of Columbus ended 31 December 1949)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hocking_Valley_Scenic_Railway (Hocking Valley Scenic Railway founded 1972; Monday Creek branch to Carbon Hill; branch scrapped 1983; present 12 mi Nelsonville-East Logan route; ex-C&O, originally Hocking Valley trackage)
metadata.rule_notes: Rule 1: this was a coal road, so the test matters here. The drawn years stop at 31 December 1949 when passenger service east of Columbus ended, though C&O freight ran on for decades and part of the line is worked today by the Indiana & Ohio. The Straitsville, Monday Creek and Snow Fork branches are coal lines with no passenger service and are not drawn at all. The Hocking Valley Scenic Railway IS drawn, from 1985, because tourist and heritage excursions count as passenger service under Rule 1 - it carries mode 'tourist_rail'. Rule 4: the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway reuses this dataset's existing #1B4D3E; the Columbus & Hocking Valley (#AA00FF), the Columbus, Hocking Valley & Toledo (#6200EA), the Hocking Valley Railway (#1A237E) and the Hocking Valley Scenic Railway (#00C853) are new to it, and each successor takes over the drawn years at the date it took over the trains.

properties.line: Columbus & Hocking Valley: Columbus – Canal Winchester
properties.speed_source: estimated: 1860s steam operation on a new coal road; estimated; no timetable consulted
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM with almost no bridging - 75.43 mi Columbus-Athens against a route documented at about 75 mi, and the intermediate distances land where the Hocking Valley's own mileposts did: Canal Winchester 15.4 mi, Lancaster 30.8, Logan 50.1, Nelsonville 62.0, Athens 75.4. Assembled from four sources chained by shared nodes: an ex-C&O belt and downtown approach through Columbus, relation 17423903 (Indiana & Ohio Logan Subdivision) for Columbus-Logan, relation 17423809 (Hocking Valley Scenic Railway) for Logan-Nelsonville, and railway=abandoned ways tagged old_railway_operator=C&O and named 'Hockhocking Adena Bikeway' - the rail-trail on the old grade - for Nelsonville-Athens. Three straight-line bridges, the largest 0.34 km. The north end stops 1.35 km short of the Columbus Union Station site and the south end 1.34 km short of the Athens depot site; both terminal areas have been rebuilt and their original trackage is not in OSM. Sliced at Canal Winchester for this feature.

segments.note: The first piece of the C&HV to open, on 16 July 1868. The company began as the Mineral Rail Road, incorporated 14 April 1864 to build Columbus-Athens; Milbury Greene, a salt works operator at Salina, bought it in 1867, talked Columbus money into finishing it, and the backers made renaming it the Columbus & Hocking Valley a condition of the finance. The point of the line was salt and coal out of the Hocking Valley, but it carried passengers from the start. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 14 April 1864 Mineral Rail Road incorporation, Greene's 1867 purchase and the naming condition, the 22 May 1867 construction contract and the 16 July 1868 opening to Canal Winchester, all from Abandoned Online.

segments.note: Opened in two steps within one year: Canal Winchester to Lancaster on 13 January 1869 and Lancaster to Nelsonville on 17 August 1869, so both fall in the same drawn year and are one feature here. Regular passenger service was running to Lancaster in 1869. The first freight train up from Nelsonville reached Columbus on 17 August 1869 with a cannon aboard, fired at each town on the way to announce it. Frequency estimated.

segments.note: The last stretch, Nelsonville to Athens, opened 25 July 1870 and completed the Columbus-Athens line the company had been chartered for. At the height of the boom three passenger trains a day ran each way between Columbus and Athens, which is the headway estimated here. The Straitsville Branch from Logan to New Straitsville followed on 2 January 1871; it and the Monday Creek and Snow Fork branches were coal lines and are not drawn, per Rule 1.

segments.note: The C&HV had no route of its own to the Lake Erie export docks, so in 1881 it consolidated with the Columbus & Toledo Railway (Columbus-Marion 1876, on to Toledo 10 January 1877) and the Ohio & West Virginia Railway (Logan-Gallipolis October 1880, Pomeroy January 1881) as the Columbus, Hocking Valley & Toledo Railway. Only the original Columbus-Athens line is drawn here; the Toledo and Gallipolis/Pomeroy lines the CHV&T also ran are not in this file. Sources disagree on the month - Abandoned Online says July 1881, Wikipedia says August 1881. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the three constituent companies and their opening dates from Abandoned Online; the consolidation month is a recorded conflict between Abandoned Online (July 1881) and Wikipedia (August 1881), neither resolved. Headway unsourced.

segments.note: The CHV&T went into receivership in 1897 and was reorganised in February 1899 as the Hocking Valley Railway. The Chesapeake & Ohio took control in March 1910 - which also gave it the Toledo & Ohio Central and the Kanawha & Michigan - but the Hocking Valley kept its own identity until 1930, so it holds this stretch to then. At the end of 1925 it worked 349 miles of road on 881 miles of track, most of the difference being coal-branch and yard trackage that is not drawn. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the 1897 receivership, February 1899 reorganisation, March 1910 C&O control and the 1925 mileage from Wikipedia; the C&O's simultaneous acquisition of the T&OC and K&M from Abandoned Online. Headway unsourced.

segments.note: The Hocking Valley was merged into the Chesapeake & Ohio on 30 April 1930 and the line became the C&O's Hocking Division. The coal seams that had justified it were thinning from the 1920s, and passenger service on the C&O's lines east of Columbus ended on 31 December 1949 - which is where this corridor's drawn years stop, though freight ran on for decades and the Columbus-Toledo line is still CSX's Columbus Subdivision. Frequency estimated at the single daily round trip the service had shrunk to; the actual last-year frequency is not sourced.
sources: Segment-level: the 30 April 1930 merger and the 31 December 1949 end of passenger service east of Columbus from the Hocking Valley Scenic Railway history and Hawkins Rails; the thinning coal traffic from Abandoned Online. Headway unsourced.

properties.line: Hocking Valley Scenic Railway: Nelsonville – East Logan
properties.speed_source: estimated: excursion speed on a preserved branch; estimated; no timetable consulted
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM relation 17423809 (Hocking Valley Scenic Railway), 12.39 mi against a documented 12 mi. No bridging. This is the same physical line as the Logan-Nelsonville portion of the Columbus-Athens features above, drawn separately because its years and operator differ.

segments.note: Passengers came back to the Hocking Valley 36 years after the C&O gave them up. The volunteer-run Hocking Valley Scenic Railway was formed in 1972 and first ran excursions over about seven miles of the old Monday Creek coal branch to Carbon Hill; when that was scrapped in 1983 it moved to the former Armitage Subdivision between Nelsonville and Glen Ebon, and from 1985 onto the present Nelsonville-East Logan route, which it later bought from the C&O to stop it being abandoned. 12 mi of former Hocking Valley, then C&O, track. Only the current route is drawn - the 1972-85 Monday Creek and Glen Ebon operations are not. Frequency estimated at a couple of round trips on an operating day; it runs weekends and seasonally, not daily, so the headway is a poor fit here.
sources: Segment-level: the 1972 founding, the Monday Creek/Carbon Hill excursions, the 1983 scrapping of that branch, the Nelsonville-Glen Ebon interim route to 1985, the move to the present route and its 12 mi length from Wikipedia and Abandoned Online. Headway unsourced and a poor fit for seasonal operation.
